syllabus.clause: Avro writer/reader schema resolution (defaults, aliases, unions)

at.step: Reveal: Protobuf doesn't match by name

syllabus.clause: Parquet's by-name vs by-position vs by-field-ID column matching

at.step: Reveal: Parquet's three ways to match a column

syllabus.clause: how table formats add stable column IDs on top (§6.3)

items.item: a reader field with a default, missing from the writer, resolves to that default
a reader field with no default, missing from the writer, is an error
a writer field not present in the reader's schema is ignored
aliases let an implementation map the writer's name to the reader's
reusing a field number makes decoding ambiguous and can lead to data corruption, not necessarily a parse error
reserved is the mechanism that prevents a future reuse of a deleted field number
SchemaElement carries an optional field_id (Thrift field 9)

Avro resolves fields by name; a reader field missing from the writer uses its default if present, or signals an error if not — this is the one load-bearing rule the chapter's own worked example depends on.
A writer field with no counterpart in the reader's schema is simply ignored, so removing a reader's interest in a field is always safe in Avro, unlike Protobuf's field-number removal.
Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, never by name; this is a completely different mechanism from Avro's name-based matching, not a variation on it.

at.step: Reveal: Protobuf doesn't match by name

items.item: Reusing a deleted Protobuf field number for a field of a different type does not raise a parse error; it silently decodes the old bytes under the new type, producing a valid-looking but wrong value.
Protobuf's reserved keyword is a compile-time guard enforced by protoc, not a runtime check; skipping it is what allows the silent corruption this topic demonstrates.
Parquet's SchemaElement carries an optional field_id; a reader that matches columns by this ID instead of name or position survives both a rename and a reordering insertion.

By-position matching fails dangerously (silently returns another column's real data) when a column is inserted anywhere but the end, while by-name matching fails safely (returns the renamed column as missing) on a rename — these are different failure modes, not degrees of the same one.

Type widening (e.g. int to a wider numeric type) and adding a nullable column are the two evolution moves every one of these formats treats as broadly safe, in contrast to a rename or a field-number/position change, which each format handles differently.

Table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake) add their own stable column-ID bookkeeping on top of a file format exactly like Parquet's field_id, which is why this topic's by-field-ID result foreshadows §6.3 rather than belonging to it.

Schema-registry compatibility modes (forward, backward, full) govern how many producers and consumers agree on compatible changes over time; this topic covers only what one reader does with one schema change, which is a prerequisite to that later topic, not a substitute for it.
